mainTopic: Hidden righteous people (אבא אומנא, the jailer, the jesters) and the laws of sounding the alarm for blight, locusts, wild beasts and armies
overview: This amud finishes the story of the רבנן who took אבא אומנא's rugs. He judged them favorably and gave the rugs to צדקה. רבא is then comforted that his merit protects his whole city. Next comes the story of רבי ברוקא and אליהו in the market, where אליהו points to people who earn עולם הבא in surprising ways: a disguised jailer, and two jesters who cheer up the sad and make peace. The גמרא then returns to the משנה's list of disasters for which the alarm is sounded everywhere, with רבי עקיבא's view that even a small sign is enough. A ברייתא explains when a dangerous beast counts as משולחת, and the גמרא settles three difficulties in it and asks why one case needed to be said at all. Finally, the גמרא starts on 'the sword': even a peaceful army passing through calls for an alarm. The proof from פרעה נכה and יאשיהו continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The רבנן take the rugs and ask אבא אומנא to appraise them
steps.stepSummary: In the morning the רבנן roll up אבא אומנא's rugs, take them to the market, and when they meet him they ask him to name their value. Then they reveal the rugs are his.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the morning they rolled up the rugs, took them, and went out to the market, and he found them. They said to him: 'Please, master, tell us how much these are worth.' He said: 'Such and such.' They said: 'Maybe they are worth more?' He said: 'That is what I paid for them.' They said: 'They are yours, and we took them from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The רבנן who had stayed at אבא אומנא's house took his rugs, and now they show them to him in the market and admit they took them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They ask him to set a price to see whether he will be angry or accuse them. He calmly gives an honest price, the same amount he paid, and he never says 'Those are mine!' His silence shows how much he trusted them.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him appraise, set a value

phrases.english: In the morning, they rolled them up and took them
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the rugs the רבנן slept on at אבא אומנא's house.

phrases.english: and they got up and went out to the market
and he found them.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: לְשַׁיְּימֵיהּ מָר הֵיכִי שָׁווּ.
phrases.english: They said to him: Let the master appraise how much they are worth.
He said to them: Such and such.
They said to him: But perhaps they are worth more?
He said to them: For this amount I bought them.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording, literally 'I took them,' meaning I bought them.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: דִּידָךְ נִיהוּ וְשַׁקְלִינְהוּ מִינָּךְ.
phrases.english: They said to him: They are yours, and we took them from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְצַפְרָא, כַּרְכִינְהוּ וְשַׁקְלִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the אבא אומנא story from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אבא אומנא stayed calm and honest even when his own property was taken.

steps.title: The רבנן ask what he suspected
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן ask אבא אומנא what he thought when he saw his rugs were missing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'Please tell us, what did you suspect us of?'
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן ask him directly what he thought about them when the rugs disappeared. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He knew they had taken the rugs but said nothing. They want to know whether he secretly thought they were thieves.

phrases.english: They said to him: Please, we beg of you,
what did you suspect us of?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמָטוּתָא מִינָּךְ בְּמַאי חֲשַׁדְתִּינַּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After revealing that they took the rugs, the רבנן ask how he understood it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What אבא אומנא assumed about the רבנן when they took his rugs.

steps.title: אבא אומנא judged them favorably
steps.stepSummary: אבא אומנא answers that he assumed they needed money quickly for פדיון שבויים and were too embarrassed to ask him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'I thought that a chance to ransom captives came up for the רבנן, and they were embarrassed to tell me.'
steps.whatsHappening: אבא אומנא explains that he never thought badly of them. He assumed they took the rugs for a great מצוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of suspecting theft, he came up with the most generous explanation possible: an urgent need to ransom captives. This is a clear example of judging others favorably.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic source for the trait of judging others favorably, even when the facts look bad.

phrases.english: He said to them: I said to myself,
an opportunity to ransom captives came up for the rabbis,
and they were embarrassed to tell me.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמֵינָא, פִּדְיוֹן שְׁבוּיִים אִיקְּלַע לְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He assumed they needed money for פדיון שבויים and were too shy to ask.

steps.title: אבא אומנא refuses to take the rugs back
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן offer to return the rugs, but אבא אומנא says he already gave them to צדקה in his mind the moment they went missing.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'Now, master, take them back!' He said to them: 'From that moment, I put them out of my mind for charity.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story of the rugs ends. אבא אומנא will not take them back because he already decided they belong to צדקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though no captives needed ransoming, he holds to the decision he made in his heart. Once he set the rugs aside for צדקה, he treats them as no longer his.

keyTerms.meaning: I removed them from my mind, gave up ownership in my thoughts

steps.whatToRemember: אבא אומנא judged the רבנן favorably and then gave up his property completely for צדקה. Both are part of why he got heavenly greetings.

phrases.english: They said to him: Now, let the master take them back!
He said to them: From that moment
I put them out of my mind for charity.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵהָהוּא שַׁעְתָּא אַסַּחְתִּינְהוּ מִדַּעְתַּאי לִצְדָקָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the rug story after his explanation.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אבא אומנא's generosity was complete. What he dedicated to צדקה in his heart he would not take back.

steps.title: רבא is comforted about אביי's greater honor
steps.stepSummary: רבא is upset that אביי received heavenly greetings more often than he did. He is told that his merit protects his whole city.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא was upset because of אביי. They said to him: 'Be satisfied that you protect the entire city.'
steps.whatsHappening: Going back to the heavenly greetings mentioned earlier, the גמרא tells how רבא felt bad and how he was comforted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי got greetings every ערב שבת, while רבא got them only on ערב יום כיפור. רבא is told that he has his own great merit: he shields the whole city.

keyTerms.meaning: It is enough for you, be satisfied

phrases.english: Rava was upset
because of Abaye,
phrases.notes: Earlier on the daf: אביי got greetings from Heaven every ערב שבת, but רבא only once a year.

phrases.english: they said to him: Be satisfied
that you protect the entire city.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲוָה קָא חָלְשָׁא דַּעְתֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא מִשּׁוּם דְּאַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the topic of heavenly greetings that introduced the אבא אומנא story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each צדיק has his own kind of merit. רבא's merit was protecting his entire city.

steps.title: רבי ברוקא asks אליהו who in the market has a share in עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: A new story: רבי ברוקא חוזאה, who often met אליהו in the market of בי לפט, asks him whether anyone there is a בן עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ברוקא חוזאה was often in the market of בי לפט. אליהו often appeared to him. He said to him: 'Is there anyone in this market who has a share in עולם הבא?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story and sets the scene. רבי ברוקא asks אליהו a question, and the answer comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story continues the theme of hidden righteous people whose greatness is not obvious. The question sets up the surprise of who אליהו will point to.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone worthy of the World to Come

phrases.english: Rabbi Beroka Ḥoza'a
was often in the market of Bei Lefet.
Elijah would often appear to him.
He said to him: Is there in this market
anyone worthy of the World to Come?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי בְּרוֹקָא חוֹזָאָה הֲוָה שְׁכִיחַ בְּשׁוּקָא דְּבֵי לָפָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new story about hidden righteous people.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether anyone in the market is a בן עולם הבא.

steps.title: אליהו says no
steps.stepSummary: אליהו answers that no one in the market is a בן עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'No.'
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו gives a first answer: nobody here. This sets up the surprise that comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The flat 'no' makes the next moment stronger. Someone does show up who is worthy, and it is not who you would expect.

phrases.english: He said to him: No.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי ברוקא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: At first, no one in the market is worthy of עולם הבא.

steps.title: A surprising man is pointed out as worthy
steps.stepSummary: Meanwhile a man passes by in black shoes and without תכלת on his garment, and אליהו says he is a בן עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile he saw a man who was wearing black shoes and did not have a תכלת thread on his garment. He said to him: 'This one is worthy of עולם הבא.'
steps.whatsHappening: אליהו points to a man who looks the least religious and says he has a share in עולם הבא. The reason will come later in the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Black shoes were not the Jewish custom, and he did not wear תכלת in his ציצית, so he looked like he was not careful. The surprise teaches that you cannot judge a person's greatness by how he looks.

keyTerms.meaning: Meanwhile, in the middle of this
Thread of תכלת, the blue thread of ציצית

steps.confusionAlert: אליהו is not praising the black shoes or the missing תכלת. The point is that this man is great despite how he looks, and the גמרא will soon explain why.

phrases.english: Meanwhile he saw a certain man
who was wearing black shoes
and did not put a thread of tekhelet on his garment.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַאי בַּר עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי הוּא.
phrases.english: He said to him: This one is worthy of the World to Come.
phrases.notes: It is אליהו speaking here, pointing out the man to רבי ברוקא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּהָכִי וְהָכִי חֲזָא לְהָהוּא גַּבְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overturns the 'no' of step 7 with a surprising exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man who looks unobservant is declared a בן עולם הבא, which teaches that greatness can be hidden.

steps.title: רבי ברוקא chases the man and asks about his work
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא runs after the man אליהו pointed out and asks what he does. The man tells him to come back tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: He ran after him and asked: What is your work? The man said: Go now, and come back tomorrow.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא wants to know why this unlikely-looking man is a בן עולם הבא, so he asks him directly. The man puts him off until tomorrow, which sets up the next scene.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is the natural follow-up to step 8: the man looks like he does not keep מצוות, yet אליהו praised him. His odd delay is a small puzzle the story will explain later, in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: What is your work / what do you do?

phrases.english: He ran after him,
phrases.notes: This is רבי ברוקא chasing the man in black shoes from step 8.

phrases.english: he said to him: What is your work?
He said to him: Go now,
and come tomorrow.

steps.triggerLanguage: רְהַט בָּתְרֵיהּ, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי עוֹבָדָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on אליהו's surprising statement about the man in black shoes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does this man do that earns him עולם הבא?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: For now, nothing. He defers until tomorrow.

steps.title: The man explains he is a jailer who protects modesty
steps.stepSummary: The next day the man explains that he is a jailer. He keeps men and women apart, and he risks his life to save Jewish women from gentiles, once by making a betrothed girl look like a נדה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next day רבי ברוקא asked again: What is your work? He answered: I am a jailer. I lock up the men separately and the women separately, and I put my bed between them so they will not come to sin. When I see a Jewish girl that gentiles have their eye on, I risk my life to save her. One day there was a betrothed girl with us whom the gentiles had their eye on. I took wine dregs and threw them on the bottom of her dress, and I said: She is a נדה.
steps.whatsHappening: The man reveals his hidden good deeds. His job puts him among gentiles, and he uses it to prevent sin and protect Jewish women.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His merit is not in outward signs but in quiet, risky acts of protection. Sleeping between the men and women means he personally guards against sin. With the wine trick, he makes the red stain look like blood, so the gentiles would think she was a נדה and leave her alone.

keyTerms.meaning: I put my life on the line

phrases.english: The next day he said to him: What is your work?
He said to him: I am a jailer,
and I lock up the men separately and the women separately,
and I place my bed between these and those,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לֵיתוֹ לִידֵי אִיסּוּרָא.
phrases.english: so that they will not come to sin.
When I see a Jewish woman
upon whom gentiles have set their eyes,
I risk my life and save her.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד הֲווֹת נַעֲרָה מְאוֹרָסָה גַּבַּן
phrases.english: One day there was a betrothed girl with us
on whom gentiles had set their eyes.
I took dregs of wine
and threw them on the bottom of her dress,
phrases.notes: The red wine stain was meant to look like blood.

phrases.english: and I said: She is menstruating.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִמְחַר אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי עוֹבָדָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 9 after the one-day delay.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He is a jailer who prevents sin among prisoners and risks his life to protect Jewish women.

steps.title: Why no ציצית and why black shoes?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא asks why the man has no ציצית threads and wears black shoes, the two things that made him look unworthy in step 8.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked him: Why do you have no threads on your garment, and why do you wear black shoes?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא now asks about the man's strange appearance, which seemed to clash with being a בן עולם הבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These were exactly the details from step 8 that made the man look like someone who does not keep מצוות. The question invites an explanation that will turn the apparent flaw into part of his merit.

phrases.english: He said to him: What is the reason
that you have no threads,
phrases.notes: He means the ציצית threads, the תכלת mentioned back in step 8.

phrases.english: and you wear black shoes?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא לֵית לָךְ חוּטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from his work to his strange dress.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why does he dress in a way that hides signs of Jewish observance?

steps.title: He hides his Jewishness to warn the רבנן about decrees
steps.stepSummary: He dresses like a gentile so no one will know he is Jewish. This lets him learn about government decrees and warn the רבנן, who pray and get the decrees cancelled.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I come and go among gentiles, so I dress this way so they won't know I am a Jew. When they issue a decree, I let the רבנן know, and they pray for mercy and the decree is cancelled.
steps.whatsHappening: The man explains that his non-Jewish look is a disguise that lets him serve the Jewish community.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What looked like a lack of observance is actually a cover. It keeps him trusted among the gentile officials, so he can hear of harsh decrees early and warn the רבנן to pray.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עָיֵילְנָא וְנָפֵיקְנָא בֵּינֵי נׇכְרִים,
phrases.english: He said to him: I come and go among gentiles,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִידְּעוּ דִּיהוּדָאָה אֲנָא.
phrases.english: so that they will not know that I am a Jew.
When they issue a decree,
I inform the Rabbis,
and they pray for mercy and cancel their decree.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: עָיֵילְנָא וְנָפֵיקְנָא בֵּינֵי נׇכְרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about his dress.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His dress is a disguise that lets him gather news of decrees and alert the רבנן.

steps.title: Why did you send me away yesterday?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא asks why the man told him the day before to go away and come back tomorrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why, when I asked you what your work was, did you tell me: Go now and come back tomorrow?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ברוקא returns to the small puzzle from step 9, the man's delay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story now closes the loop on the man's odd behavior. The answer will connect the delay to the job he just described.

phrases.aramaic: וּמַאי טַעְמָא כִּי אָמֵינָא לָךְ אֲנָא
phrases.english: And what is the reason that when I said to you,
'What is your work,'

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַרְתְּ לִי: זִיל הָאִידָּנָא וְתָא לִמְחַר?
phrases.english: you said to me: Go now and come tomorrow?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי טַעְמָא כִּי אָמֵינָא לָךְ אֲנָא מַאי עוֹבָדָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the delay from step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why did he put off answering the day before?

steps.title: A decree had just been issued, so he rushed to warn the רבנן
steps.stepSummary: At that very moment a decree had been issued, and he needed to hurry and alert the רבנן to pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: At that very hour they had issued a decree. I said to myself: First I will go and pass it on, and send word to the רבנן so they will pray for mercy about it.
steps.whatsHappening: The man explains that he was busy saving the community at that moment, so he could not stop to talk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even his delay was a good deed. He put the urgent needs of the community before a conversation with a great רב.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּהַהִיא שַׁעְתָּא גָּזְרִי גְּזֵירְתָּא,
phrases.english: He said to him: At that moment they had issued a decree,
and I said: First I will go and make it known,
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is the corrected wording. It adds 'it,' so he means he'll make the decree known.

phrases.english: and I will send word to the Rabbis
so that they will pray for mercy about the matter.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בְּהַהִיא שַׁעְתָּא גָּזְרִי גְּזֵירְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the delay.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He was rushing to warn the רבנן about a new decree.

steps.title: Two brothers arrive, and אליהו says they too merit עולם הבא
steps.stepSummary: Two brothers come by, and אליהו tells רבי ברוקא that they are also בני עולם הבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile, two brothers came by. אליהו said to him: These too are people of עולם הבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to a second example of surprising people who merit עולם הבא. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'too' links them to the jailer. Once again אליהו points to people who look ordinary, and רבי ברוקא will need to ask what makes them special.

phrases.aramaic: אַדְּהָכִי וְהָכִי אֲתוֹ הָנָךְ תְּרֵי אַחֵי.
phrases.english: Meanwhile, these two brothers came.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנָךְ נָמֵי בְּנֵי עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי נִינְהוּ.
phrases.english: He said to him: These too are people of the World to Come.
phrases.notes: The speaker is אליהו, talking to רבי ברוקא.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּהָכִי וְהָכִי אֲתוֹ הָנָךְ תְּרֵי אַחֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels step 8 with a second surprising pair.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two brothers also have a share in עולם הבא.

steps.title: רבי ברוקא asks the brothers about their work
steps.stepSummary: רבי ברוקא goes over to the brothers and asks what they do.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went over to them and asked: What is your work?
steps.whatsHappening: Just as with the jailer, רבי ברוקא asks the brothers what they do to merit עולם הבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The repeated question shows the pattern of the story. The answer always lies in what a person actually does, not how they look.

phrases.english: He went over to them,
he said to them: What is your work?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲזַל לְגַבַּיְיהוּ, אֲמַר לְהוּ: מַאי עוֹבָדַיְיכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on אליהו's statement about the brothers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What do the brothers do that earns them עולם הבא?

steps.title: The brothers cheer up sad people and make peace
steps.stepSummary: The brothers are jesters who cheer up sad people, and they work to make peace between people who are quarreling.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: We are cheerful people, and we cheer up those who are sad. Also, when we see two people who are fighting, we put in effort and make peace between them.
steps.whatsHappening: The brothers explain their simple but powerful deeds: bringing joy and bringing peace. This ends the story of רבי ברוקא and אליהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their merit comes from caring about other people's feelings and relationships. The story teaches that such everyday kindness can earn עולם הבא, just like the jailer's risky acts.

keyTerms.meaning: We take trouble, we work hard

steps.whatToRemember: The people אליהו pointed to as בני עולם הבא did not look special. A disguised jailer and two jesters earned their reward through hidden protection of others, bringing joy, and making peace.

phrases.english: They said to him: We are cheerful people,
we cheer up the sad.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי, כִּי חָזֵינַן בֵּי תְרֵי
phrases.english: Also, when we see two people
who have a quarrel between them,
we work hard and make peace between them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: אִינָשֵׁי בָּדוֹחֵי אֲנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question to the brothers and closes the story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They cheer up sad people and make peace between people who are fighting.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: calamities for which they sound the alarm everywhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's line about sounding the alarm in every place, and quotes a ברייתא that lists the calamities: blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, and dangerous beasts.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'For these they sound the alarm in every place, etc.' The רבנן taught in a ברייתא: For these they sound the alarm in every place: for blight, for mildew, for locusts and caterpillars, and for dangerous beasts.
steps.whatsHappening: The story is over, and the גמרא goes back to the next line of the משנה. It brings a ברייתא that spells out which disasters call for an alarm everywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'In every place' means that even communities that are not hit yet sound the alarm, because these disasters can spread. The ברייתא gives the basic list, and רבי עקיבא's opinion will follow.

keyTerms.meaning: They sound the alarm (with fasting, prayer, and blowing)

phrases.aramaic: עַל אֵלּוּ מַתְרִיעִין בְּכׇל מָקוֹם כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: "For these they sound the alarm in every place, etc."
The Rabbis taught:
For these they sound the alarm in every place:
for blight, and for mildew,
and for locusts and caterpillars,
and for dangerous beasts.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל אֵלּוּ מַתְרִיעִין בְּכׇל מָקוֹם כּוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadah and returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillars, and dangerous beasts, the alarm is sounded in every place.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: even a tiny amount is enough
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא says that for blight and mildew, any amount calls for an alarm. For locusts, even one wing seen anywhere in ארץ ישראל is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: For blight and mildew, they sound the alarm over any amount. For locusts and caterpillars, even if only one wing was seen in all of ארץ ישראל, they sound the alarm.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא adds a stricter standard for how much of the disaster is needed before sounding the alarm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא listed which disasters count. רבי עקיבא addresses how much is needed and says the smallest sign is enough. A single wing is treated as a warning that a whole swarm may be coming.

keyTerms.meaning: In any amount, even the smallest

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַשִּׁדָּפוֹן וְעַל הַיֵּרָקוֹן בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא.
phrases.english: For blight and for mildew, over any amount.
Locusts and caterpillars:
even if nothing was seen in the Land of Israel
except a single wing,
they sound the alarm over them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אוֹמֵר: עַל הַשִּׁדָּפוֹן וְעַל הַיֵּרָקוֹן בְּכׇל שֶׁהוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds רבי עקיבא's view on the amount needed for the calamities just listed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any amount of blight or mildew, or even one locust wing seen in ארץ ישראל, is enough to sound the alarm.

steps.title: A dangerous beast only calls for an alarm when it is an outbreak
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words about beasts and brings a ברייתא: an alarm is sounded only when the beast is משולחת. Being seen in the city or by day counts as משולחת. Being seen in the field or at night does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the משנה's line on beasts, the רבנן taught: the dangerous beast they mentioned only calls for an alarm when it is an outbreak. Which counts as an outbreak? If it is seen in the city, yes. In the field, no. By day, yes. At night, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next item in the משנה, dangerous beasts. It quotes a ברייתא that says an alarm is sounded only when the beast is acting abnormally, called משולחת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא first sets the rule: no alarm for a normal wild animal, only for one that is משולחת. It then lists signs. A beast in its natural place (the field) or at its natural time (night) is not unusual. A beast in a town or out in daylight is.

phrases.english: "And for a beast, etc."
The Rabbis taught:
The dangerous beast that they mentioned,
when it is an outbreak —
phrases.notes: Literally "sent out." It means the beast is out of control and not behaving the normal way.

phrases.english: they sound the alarm over it;
if it is not an outbreak, they do not sound the alarm over it.
Which counts as an outbreak
and which does not count as an outbreak?
If it is seen in the city, it is an outbreak;
in the field, it is not an outbreak.
By day, it is an outbreak;
at night, it is not an outbreak.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַל חַיָּה וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא's list and רבי עקיבא's view on how much blight, mildew and locusts are needed, the גמרא takes up the משנה's words about dangerous beasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An alarm is sounded for a beast only when it is משולחת. City and day are signs of משולחת. Field and night are not.

steps.title: More signs of an abnormal beast: chasing, killing without eating, taking a baby
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with behavior signs. Chasing people, killing two but eating one, or snatching a baby from a roof all count as משולחת. Hiding, or eating both victims, does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it saw two people and chased them, it is an outbreak. If it hid from them, it is not. If it killed two people and ate one, it is an outbreak. If it ate both, it is not. If it climbed onto a roof and took a baby from its cradle, it is an outbreak.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going and gives more signs, this time based on how the beast acts toward people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the beast acts like a normal hungry animal or attacks beyond its nature. Eating both victims looks like ordinary hunger. Killing two and eating only one, chasing people, or climbing a roof for a baby shows unnatural aggression.

phrases.english: If it saw two people
and ran after them, it is an outbreak.
If it hid from them, it is not an outbreak.
If it tore apart two people
and ate one of them, it is an outbreak.
If it ate both of them, it is not an outbreak.
If it climbed up to the roof
and took a baby from a cradle, it is an outbreak.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָאֲתָה שְׁנֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם וְרָצְתָה אַחֲרֵיהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, adding behavior-based signs to the place-and-time signs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Aggressive behavior beyond normal hunger (chasing, killing without eating, snatching a baby from a roof) makes the beast משולחת.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself about a beast in the city at night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא first says any beast seen in the city is משולחת, day or night. Then it says that at night it is not משולחת. These seem to clash.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא contradicts itself. You said that if it is seen in the city it is an outbreak, with no difference between day and night. Then you said that by day it is an outbreak and at night it is not!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא for contradicting itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line "seen in the city is an outbreak" sounds like a full rule that includes nighttime. The very next line says nighttime is never an outbreak. So a beast in the city at night gets two opposite answers.

keyTerms.meaning: This text itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
You said: if it was seen in the city, it is an outbreak;
no difference whether by day
and no difference whether at night.
And then you said:
By day, it is an outbreak;
at night, it is not an outbreak!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא גּוּפַהּ קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After quoting the whole ברייתא, the גמרא goes back to its first signs and finds an internal contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's signs of city/field and day/night in step 20
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: "City means outbreak" implies even at night, but "night means not an outbreak" implies even in the city. A beast in the city at night gets two opposite rulings.

steps.title: The signs work together: only city plus daytime counts as an outbreak
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא's signs should be read together. City by day is משולחת. City at night is not. A field, even by day, is not, and certainly not at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This is what the ברייתא means: seen in the city by day, it is an outbreak. In the city at night, it is not. And in the field, even by day, it is not an outbreak.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction by explaining that the ברייתא's two signs are meant to be combined, not read as separate rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both signs are needed together. The beast must be in the city and also out in daytime to count as משולחת. If either one is missing, it is not an outbreak. That removes the contradiction.
steps.whatToRemember: A beast counts as משולחת (calling for an alarm) only when it is seen in the city by day, or when it shows unnatural aggression. In the field, or at night, it is acting normally.

phrases.english: It is not difficult. This is what it is saying:
If it was seen in the city by day, it is an outbreak.
In the city at night, it is not an outbreak.
Alternatively, in the field,
phrases.notes: Here it just adds the next case on the same scale. It does not offer a second answer.

phrases.english: even by day, it is not an outbreak.
(In the field at night, it is not an outbreak.)
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 22 by rereading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the ברייתא's wording (הכי קאמר): the two signs are combined, not separate
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each sign stands alone: city alone means outbreak, and night alone means no outbreak, so they clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both conditions are required together. City and day is an outbreak. City at night, or a field at any time, is not.

steps.title: A beast that just stands there: two clashing inferences
steps.stepSummary: From one line of the ברייתא we learn that a standing beast is not משולחת. From another line we learn that it is. The גמרא points out the clash.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא says that if the beast saw two people and ran after them, it is משולחת. That implies that if it only stood there, it is not. Then the ברייתא says that if it hid from them, it is not משולחת. That implies that if it only stood there, it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finds a second contradiction inside the same ברייתא. This time the question is about a beast that neither chases nor hides, but simply stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each line of the ברייתא gives a clear case, but each also hints at the middle case of standing still. The chasing line hints that standing is not enough to be dangerous. The hiding line hints that standing is already a dangerous sign. The two hints cannot both be true as they stand.

keyTerms.meaning: This implies; it points to what follows from the words
It stands still, neither chasing nor running away
And then you said; it brings a later line that seems to clash

steps.confusionAlert: Neither line of the ברייתא actually mentions standing. Both 'standing' rulings are inferences the גמרא draws from what each line leaves out.

phrases.english: If it saw two people
and ran after them, it is on the loose.
This implies that if it stands, it is not on the loose.
And then you said:
If it hid from them, it is not on the loose.
This implies that if it stands, it is on the loose!

steps.triggerLanguage: וַהֲדַר אָמְרַתְּ: נֶחְבֵּאת מִפְּנֵיהֶן — אֵינָהּ מְשׁוּלַּחַת, הָא עוֹמֶדֶת — מְשׁוּלַּחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling the city/field and day/night clash in Steps 22-23, the גמרא raises a new clash from the behavior signs in the ברייתא (Step 21).
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's two behavior signs: chasing, and hiding
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading each line for what it leaves out gives opposite rulings for a beast that simply stands still.

steps.title: It depends on whether a marsh is nearby
steps.stepSummary: The two inferences are about different places. One is about a field next to a marsh. The other is about a field far from a marsh.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. One line is about a field next to a marsh. The other line is about a field that is not next to a marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash by placing each inference in a different kind of field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Next to a marsh, a beast can easily escape into its hiding place, so simply standing calmly is not a bold act. Only chasing people shows it is dangerous. Far from a marsh it has nowhere to flee, so standing its ground in front of people already shows unusual boldness.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; this opens an answer
Here... here; each source is talking about a different case
Marsh or swamp, a natural hiding place for wild animals

steps.whatToRemember: Standing still near a marsh is not a sign of danger. Standing still in a field far from a marsh is.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
Here, it is in a field next to a marsh,
there, it is in a field not next to a marsh.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן — בְּשָׂדֶה הַסְּמוּכָה לַאֲגַם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each inference applies in a different location
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both inferences seemed to rule on the very same case of a beast standing still.
steps.terutzMaskana: Near a marsh, standing is not משולחת. Far from a marsh, standing is משולחת.

steps.title: Why require killing if chasing is already enough?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says that killing two people and eating only one is a sign of a beast on the loose. The גמרא asks why this is needed, since chasing alone was already enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא says that if it tore apart two people at once and ate one of them, it is משולחת. If it ate both, it is not. But didn't you say that even running after people is enough?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the killing sign from the ברייתא and challenges it with the chasing sign from earlier in the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a beast that merely chased people already counts as משולחת, then a beast that actually killed two people should count all the more. So why does the ברייתא need the detail of eating only one, and why does eating both make it not משולחת? The killing case looks either unnecessary or in conflict with the chasing case.

keyTerms.meaning: It tore apart, it attacked and killed
But didn't you say? This brings up an earlier statement as a challenge

phrases.english: If it tore apart two people at once
and ate one of them, it is on the loose;
if it ate both of them, it is not on the loose.
But didn't you say that even if it only ran after them, it is on the loose!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אָמְרַתְּ אֲפִילּוּ רָצְתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving the standing clash, the גמרא raises a new difficulty between two other signs in the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a beast which kills two people and eats one is משולחת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Chasing alone is already enough, so requiring killing, and excusing a beast that ate both, makes no sense.

steps.title: רב פפא: the killing case is in a marsh
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the killing case is about a beast in a marsh, where chasing alone would not be a sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: when that case is taught, it is about a beast in a marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the challenge by placing the killing case in a different setting from the chasing case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A marsh is the beast's own home, so attacking people who come there is normal behavior, and even chasing them proves nothing. That is why only a stronger sign counts there: killing two and eating just one, which shows it kills for more than food. Outside the marsh, chasing alone is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: When that teaching was taught; it limits a source to a specific case
Marsh, the Aramaic form of אֲגַם

steps.whatToRemember: In a marsh, the beast's home, only killing more than it eats shows it is משולחת. Elsewhere, chasing is enough.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
When that case is taught, it is about a marsh.
phrases.notes: 'That case' is the beast that tore apart two people. In the marsh it is on its home turf.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי תָּנֵי הָהִיא, בְּאַגְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the killing case is limited to a marsh
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The killing case seemed to apply everywhere, which made the chasing case contradict it.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a marsh, a stronger sign is needed. Elsewhere, chasing alone shows the beast is משולחת.

steps.title: Back to the ברייתא: a baby taken from a roof, isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא's case of a beast that climbed onto a roof and took a baby from its cradle, and asks why this needed to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the ברייתא itself: if it climbed onto the roof and took a baby from its cradle, it is משולחת. That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another line from the ברייתא and challenges it as too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A beast that climbs onto a house and snatches a baby is clearly acting wildly and dangerously. So why would the ברייתא bother to teach this case? The challenge sets up a search for a setting where the case is not so obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter itself; the גמרא returns to look closely at a source it already quoted
It is obvious! Why did this need to be said?

phrases.english: Back to the text itself:
phrases.notes: This returns to the ברייתא from Step 21 to look at one of its lines.

phrases.aramaic: עָלְתָה לַגַּג וְנָטְלָה תִּינוֹק מֵעֲרִיסָה — מְשׁוּלַּחַת.
phrases.english: If it climbed to the roof and took a baby from a cradle, it is on the loose.
That's obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא: עָלְתָה לַגַּג וְנָטְלָה תִּינוֹק מֵעֲרִיסָה — מְשׁוּלַּחַת. פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of Step 21 to examine a line not yet discussed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's case of a beast snatching a baby from a roof
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case is so clearly dangerous that teaching it seems pointless.

steps.title: רב פפא: the roof of a hunters' hut
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the roof was of a hunters' hut out in the wild, where an attack might have seemed natural.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: it is talking about something like the huts of hunters.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the 'obvious' challenge by setting the case in a place where it is not so obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hunters' huts stand out in the wilderness, in the beasts' own area. One might think a beast attacking there is just acting normally. So the ברייתא teaches that even there, snatching a baby from the roof shows the beast is משולחת.
steps.whatToRemember: Even in the wild, at a hunters' hut, a beast that takes a baby from the roof is משולחת.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Like the huts of hunters.
phrases.notes: He means the roof in the ברייתא belonged to a hut out in the wild, not a house in town.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כְּכוּכֵי דְצַיָּידֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of Step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Setting the case in a specific place (אוקימתא) so that it teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without this, one might think an attack at a hut in the wild is normal behavior for a beast.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even at a hunters' hut in the wild, taking a baby from the roof makes the beast משולחת.

steps.title: Even a peaceful army is a reason to sound the alarm
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of 'the sword'. A ברייתא says this obviously includes an enemy army, and it also includes an army that is only passing through in peace.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said we sound the alarm for the sword. The רבנן taught: the 'sword' they mentioned is not only an army coming to fight us. That is obvious. It even includes a 'sword of peace', an army just passing through.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to a new line of the משנה, 'the sword', and brings a ברייתא that explains how wide this rule is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An army attacking us is clearly a danger, so the ברייתא calls that case obvious. The new point is that even an army with no plan to fight us is enough to sound the alarm. The ברייתא's proof comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Sword. Here it means an army or war.
A 'sword of peace': an army passing through that is not coming to fight us
The Sages taught. This opens a ברייתא.
It goes without saying. The obvious case comes first, then the bigger point.

steps.confusionAlert: A 'sword of peace' does not mean a friendly army that helps us. It means an army that is busy with someone else and is only passing through our land.

phrases.english: "For the sword, etc."
The Sages taught:
The sword that they mentioned,
it is not necessary to say
a sword that is not of peace,
rather, even a sword of peace.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל הַחֶרֶב וְכוּ׳. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of wild beasts and moves to the next case in the משנה, the sword.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We sound the alarm even for an army that is only passing through and not coming to fight.

steps.title: Proof from פרעה נכה and King יאשיהו
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא proves its point: no army was more of a 'sword of peace' than פרעה נכה, yet King יאשיהו still came to harm because of it. A פסוק is introduced as the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no better example of a peaceful army than פרעה נכה. Even so, King יאשיהו stumbled because of it, as the פסוק says:
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא backs up its rule with a story from תנ״ך and starts to quote the פסוק. The פסוק itself comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: פרעה נכה's army was only passing through, so it is the clearest case of a 'sword of peace'. Even so, it led to the downfall of a righteous king, יאשיהו. This shows that a passing army is also a real danger, so we sound the alarm for it too.

keyTerms.meaning: פרעה נכה, a king of Egypt whose army passed through ארץ ישראל
King יאשיהו, a righteous king of יהודה
As it is said. This introduces a פסוק.

steps.whatToRemember: Even an army that is not aiming at us is a danger, so we sound the alarm for it. The proof is פרעה נכה, who brought harm to King יאשיהו.

phrases.english: for you have no sword of peace
greater than Pharaoh Neco,
phrases.notes: His army was passing through on the way to fight someone else, not us.

phrases.english: and even so
King Josiah stumbled because of it,
as it is said:

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁאֵין לְךָ חֶרֶב שֶׁל שָׁלוֹם יוֹתֵר מִפַּרְעֹה נְכֹה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the proof for the ruling in step 30, that even a sword of peace counts.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that we sound the alarm even for a 'sword of peace'
